passage:
In Barshi, Kiran spent mornings at college, afternoons behind the counter of the family's seed shop, and nights with a torch over accounts textbooks. Exams started Monday. Amma's knee was getting worse and the monsoon was late, so sales were down. Kiran thought about all of it at once, all the time.
On Thursday Salma, a regular customer, paid for two bags of seed. Kiran gave her change for a hundred instead of fifty. She came back smiling and returned the extra. "You're somewhere else today."
That night Kiran filled in the practice form and wrote the wrong roll number twice. Kiran's head felt full of cotton.
Salma's words stuck. The next morning Kiran wrote a list: shop hours cut to three days till exams, a cousin to cover, one worry at a time.

qa.q: What mistake did Kiran make with Salma's change?
qa.a: Kiran gave her change for a hundred instead of fifty.

qa.q: What was Kiran feeling on the night of the wrong roll number?
qa.a: Kiran felt foggy and overloaded, head full of cotton, because exams, the shop and worries about Amma and the rain were all taking up space at once.

qa.q: Is Kiran's list a good response?
qa.a: Yes; cutting shop hours, asking a cousin to cover and taking one worry at a time frees some mental space, which should cut down the careless mistakes.

qa.q: How did Salma see Kiran that day?
qa.a: Salma noticed Kiran was distracted and "somewhere else", and responded kindly by returning the money with a smile.

grounding: It shows a student juggling exams, shop work and family worries who makes careless mistakes and feels foggy because stress uses up mental capacity.

passage:
In Porto, Ivan had three exams in five days, four evening shifts at the café near the university, and a letter about his residence permit renewal that he kept rereading at night. By Wednesday he was running on coffee and dread.
At the café he rang up a cappuccino as a latte, then forgot a table entirely. Beatriz, his shift partner, quietly fixed both. At home he emailed his statistics assignment to his economics professor.
"You look like a phone with too many apps open," Beatriz said at closing.
"I'm fine. I just need to push through."
"You're not dumb, you're full." She took his notepad and wrote three things: swap Friday shift, call the international office about the permit, exam first.
Ivan read the list twice. It was the first thing all week that let him breathe out.

qa.q: Where did Ivan send his statistics assignment?
qa.a: He emailed his statistics assignment to his economics professor.

qa.q: Why does Ivan insist he just needs to push through?
qa.a: He probably feels he should cope alone and doesn't see the mistakes as a sign of overload; admitting it might feel like weakness.

qa.q: Why does Beatriz's three-item list help?
qa.a: It takes the permit worry and an extra shift off his mind, so his limited attention can go to the exam first.

qa.q: How does Beatriz see Ivan's mistakes?
qa.a: Beatriz sees them as a sign he is overloaded, not careless or dumb, like a phone with too many apps open.

grounding: It shows a student juggling exams, work and a permit worry who makes careless mistakes because stress takes up part of his limited capacity.

passage:
By the second week of placements, the hostel corridor smelled of instant coffee and panic. Chinmay had two interviews, a final-year project review, and a phone that buzzed with updates about his grandfather in hospital back in Nagpur.
On Tuesday he submitted the project report with last semester's circuit diagram. On Wednesday he locked his room key inside twice. On Thursday he walked into the wrong interview hall and stood there, blank.
Eshaan, his roommate, found him on the hostel steps that night. "You're making mistakes you never make."
"I'm so stupid right now."
"Not stupid. You're carrying too much at once." Eshaan sat beside him. "Tell me everything that's in your head. We'll write it down."
They filled a page. Seeing it on paper, Chinmay cried a little, then circled the one task for tomorrow.

qa.q: What did Chinmay submit with the project report?
qa.a: He submitted it with last semester's circuit diagram.

qa.q: Why does Chinmay call himself stupid?
qa.a: He is shocked by mistakes he never usually makes and blames himself, not seeing that worry about his grandfather and the pile of tasks are using up his attention.

qa.q: How did writing everything down help Chinmay?
qa.a: Putting it on paper moved the load out of his head, let some feelings out, and left him with just one task for tomorrow.

qa.q: How does Eshaan see Chinmay's week?
qa.a: Eshaan sees a capable roommate who is overloaded, not stupid, and chooses to sit beside him and help instead of judging.

grounding: It shows a student juggling placements, a project and family worry who makes careless mistakes and feels foggy as stress uses up his capacity.

passage:
Dear Francis,
Sorry I missed your birthday call. My brain is soup these days. Exams all month, evening shifts at the hotel front desk, and Mai's shop has been slow, so I keep checking its accounts at midnight.
This week I did three stupid things. I booked two families into the same room at the hotel, and the manager had to sort it out. I wrote my roll number wrong on Monday's accounts paper and had to run to the exam office. And yesterday I put sugar in the dal instead of salt. Mai, my mother, laughed, but I didn't.
I'm not careless, you know me. It's like my head is full and every new thing spills out.
Write when you can.
Samir

qa.q: What happened at the hotel this week?
qa.a: Samir booked two families into the same room, and the manager had to sort it out.

qa.q: How does Samir feel about the mistakes?
qa.a: Samir feels frustrated and a little scared, insisting "I'm not careless" while describing a head so full that new things spill out.

qa.q: What small step could Samir take to lighten the load during exams?
qa.a: Samir could ask the hotel for fewer shifts this month and pick one fixed time to check the shop accounts instead of every midnight, freeing some room in a crowded mind.

qa.q: What might Mai have been thinking when she laughed at the sweet dal?
qa.a: She probably laughed to ease the moment, but may also have noticed how stretched and tired Samir is, and felt worried.

grounding: A student juggling exams, a job and family worries writes about careless mistakes and a foggy, overfull mind.

passage: Lakshmi, you asked what that November was like. Honestly? Fog. I had semester exams, four online tutoring sessions a night to help at home since Baba lost his job, and a head full of "what if we can't pay the hostel fee". I thought I was managing. Then the mistakes started. I uploaded my cousin's birthday video instead of my lab report. In the circuits quiz I wrote milliamps where it should have been amps, on every single answer. One night I taught a Class 8 boy the wrong formula for area, and his mother messaged me the next day. I'm Bidisha, the girl who used to find everyone else's errors. That November I couldn't find my own. It wasn't that I didn't know the stuff. There just wasn't room left in my head.

qa.q: What did Bidisha upload instead of the lab report?
qa.a: Her cousin's birthday video.

qa.q: Why does Bidisha say it wasn't that she didn't know the stuff?
qa.a: She knew the material, but worry about money and too many jobs filled her mind, so there was no room left to catch errors 😔

qa.q: What could Bidisha have tried that November to clear some of the fog?
qa.a: She could have spoken to her tutor or a college counsellor about the pressure, dropped a tutoring session or two during exams, and used a short checklist before submitting work.

qa.q: How might the mother of the Class 8 boy see Bidisha's mistake?
qa.a: She would likely be worried about her son's homework and may have doubted the tutor, without knowing how stretched Bidisha was.

grounding: A student recalls how exams, night work and money worries used up her mental space and led to careless mistakes.
